module_title: Talaq, Shayara Bano Case & Dissolution of Marriages Act
introduction: This intermediate tier explores the modes of dissolution of a Muslim marriage. It highlights the distinction between approved (Sunnat) and disapproved (Biddat) forms of Talaq, the historic criminalization of Triple Talaq, and the statutory rights of women to seek divorce.

core_concepts.title: Talaq by Husband (Extra-Judicial)
core_concepts.description:
A Muslim husband of sound mind who has attained puberty may divorce his wife without assigning any cause.
1. Talaq-ul-Sunnat (Approved Form): Can be revoked. 
   - *Ahsan*: A single pronouncement during 'Tuhr' (period between menstruations) followed by abstinence during the Iddat period. Most approved form.
   - *Hasan*: Three pronouncements made during three successive Tuhrs, with no intercourse during any of the three. It becomes irrevocable on the third pronouncement.

core_concepts.title: Talaq-ul-Biddat (Triple Talaq) & Shayara Bano Case
core_concepts.description:
Talaq-ul-Biddat is the utterance of 'Talaq' three times in a single breath/sentence. It was irrevocable immediately.
- The Landmark Case: In *Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017)*, a 5-judge Supreme Court bench struck down Triple Talaq as unconstitutional and manifestly arbitrary (violative of Article 14).
- The 2019 Act: The Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019 criminalized the pronouncement of Triple Talaq, making it a cognizable, non-bailable offense punishable with up to **3 years imprisonment**.

core_concepts.title: Divorce by Mutual Consent (Khula and Mubarat)
core_concepts.description:
- Khula: Divorce at the instance of the *wife*. The wife agrees to give consideration (usually releasing her Mahr) to the husband for her release from the marriage tie.
- Mubarat: Divorce by *mutual consent* where the aversion is mutual. Both parties desire separation equally. Neither party is legally bound to pay consideration.

core_concepts.title: The Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act, 1939
core_concepts.description:
Before 1939, a Muslim woman had very limited grounds to seek judicial divorce. This Act gave Muslim women the statutory right to seek a decree of divorce from the court on specific grounds (Section 2):
- Husband's whereabouts unknown for 4 years.
- Failure to maintain the wife for 2 years.
- Husband sentenced to imprisonment for 7 years or more.
- Cruelty (physical or mental).
- Impotency of the husband.

important_entities.name: Option of Puberty (Khyar-ul-Bulugh)
important_entities.key_fact: Right to repudiate a child marriage.
important_entities.significance: If a Muslim girl was given in marriage by her guardian (father/grandfather) before she attained the age of 15, she has the absolute right to repudiate the marriage before turning 18, provided the marriage was not consummated. This is codified in the Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act, 1939.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: A common misconception is that a Muslim wife cannot pronounce Talaq. While the power of Talaq originally belongs to the husband, he can delegate this power to his wife or any third party at the time of marriage or later. This is called **Talaq-e-Tafweez** (Delegated Divorce), and the wife can use it to divorce herself without going to court.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Associate Biddat with 'Banned' following the 2017 Shayara Bano judgment and 2019 legislation.

exam_strategy_tips: If an exam asks 'In which form of mutual divorce does the initial offer strictly come from the wife, involving a release of dower?', the answer is **Khula**.
